title: Comparison of addition variants (cls, step_fork, step_ar, ar, addressed_step_ar, addressed_ar)
question: Across the six addition variants—step-harnessed parallel classification (`cls`), parallel query branches (`step_fork`), sequential step predictions (`step_ar`), and addressed step predictions (`addressed_step_ar`, defaulting to `nope`), alongside pure-LM full-trace generation (`ar` and `addressed_ar`, operating strictly on `input_ids` with zero side-channel metadata)—how do convergence speed, in-domain accuracy, and zero-shot base and length transfer compare? In particular: (1) why do `cls` (3 linear heads) and `step_ar` (sequential conditioning) outperform `step_fork` (3 independent tied-head queries), and (2) under `input_ids`-only (`nope`), does continuous 1-hop rollout in `ar` and `addressed_ar` avoid the cold-counting bottleneck of `step_ar --embedding-mode nope`? (Note on training budgets: `train.jsonl` logs `loss` in normalised `nats / target` alongside cumulative supervised `tokens_seen`; at fixed `batch_size = 64` on `L = 1..20`, full-trace `ar` and `addressed_ar` supervise all `K + 1` columns per problem—`~14x` more column transitions per optimiser step than single-step `cls` / `step_fork` / `step_ar` / `addressed_step_ar`.)
